113.t: No horn, so teaching himself piano from records
113.s: His poor family never bought the horn the band teacher suggested, so he picked up the piano by ear, hit and miss.
113.q: Yes we had a piano around the house, and you know like back in your high school days, the band teacher was trying to get my folks to get me a horn but the folks was poor back then in those days you know, I mean really poor. So I never did get the horn.

113.t: Teaching his sister's piano piece and picking out tunes
113.s: He showed his sister a piece at her lesson; the teacher told his mother he was getting free lessons, but there was no money, so he taught himself by ear at about ten.
113.q: horn. It didn't make any difference, you know. I said, "This is the way this goes," and I…

19.t: Cutting lessons for the movies, then returning to the teacher
19.s: He skips lessons for the Howard Theatre, is stopped by his father, asks to go back, and the teacher marvels at what he learned by ear.
19.ch: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
19.q: I went to Mr. Boyd for I guess maybe four or five months. And, like all youngsters, you learn a little bit of something and you think you know something. Meanwhile, I was at home. I was playing every day, playing what he had taught me and trying to go beyond that, finding other chords and learning

19.t: Jack Smith's one and only lesson
19.s: His father hires Jack Smith as teacher, then dismisses him on the spot because he arrived drunk and taught without music.
19.ch: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
19.q: So, if I can digress a little bit, oh, about six or seven months after my uncle and my father brought this piano to the house, I had been coming in every evening, sitting and playing, and no one ever had to tell me to practice or anything like that. So they just let me play as much as I wanted to.…

115.t: The roomer pianist who let him sit in
115.s: A talented pianist rooming in the same house let Gus beat on his drum along with him, until the man lost his mind.
115.ch: Childhood in Tyler, Beaumont and Houston
115.q: Right, I'd not be humming anything, just be playing by myself. And it happened, where we were staying there was a guy that lived in one of the rooms. We were rooming in those places.

115.t: Piano lessons from the rooming-house pianist; bass came later
115.s: The roomer gave him his first piano lessons, scales and chords, though piano was not his bag; the bass came around 1935.
115.q: And he started me out, learning to play the piano, yeah. Like your first lesson, (singing).

118.s: His father played a little piano; Williams began at five, learned by watching his mother, never read music, and played nickel house parties.
118.q: Like something about a catch, you know. He always had a piano at home. My mother really was able. And I liked playing for my mother. Which I was a kid, five years old, playing piano.

150.t: Piano lessons abandoned for sandlot baseball
150.s: He took a few piano lessons but preferred sports, playing first base for the Algiers Giants and the Gretna All-Stars under Wesley Barrow.

620.t: Learning piano from brother Juby, no lessons
620.s: He picked up piano around age ten from his older brother Juby, never took lessons, and played ragtime and blues, making each piece his own way.

712.t: Teaching herself piano; her mother's rule
712.s: No musicians in her family; she taught herself from a found book of waltzes, took brief lessons and one year of college music.
712.q: No. Nobody, I never heard of anybody in my family ever singing a note or playing a note or anything. 628.t: Rehearsing with a white family band
628.s: Williams recalls rehearsing with a white neighbour, guitarist Paul Lane, whose sister played bass and who played Dixieland, and a pianist named Oscar Pierce.
628.ch: Joseph Thomas band and house parties
628.q: I used to rehearse with the next door neighbor. His sister played bass, played one of them bass. He played Dixieland music, you know. And the other fella they called Oscar, Oscar Pierce, he played piano.

760.q: Oh, yeah. So anyway, then after I came out of school, I still didn't play the piano. I was great about playing baseball and I become a ball player.

155.t: Early piano lessons in Halifax and getting the movie-theatre job

834.s: Good ears but no natural technique; piano lessons with a jazz-loving teacher; hard work translating bebop language to the horn.
834.q: I did have good ears, but I did not have a naturally great technique. I was slipping and sliding like everybody else. 153.s: Working the store taught him classical and jazz repertoire; his father pointed him to piano for theory and harmony, leading to ensemble writing and the chart he is finishing now.
153.q: All kinds of music, because I was geared to that in the music store. Somebody would come in and say, “I want something by Stravinsky.” I’d get the book out, get the records out. That’s how I learned classical music.

491.q: Oh yes. The book I remember, to help you with your scales and your velocity, Czerny – Czerny studies. Spelled C-z-n-e-r-y, I think. And then the Hannon studies. Then you had the etudes. 371.t: The player piano and teacher Pauline McCann
371.s: The family player piano and rolls fascinated him; his first teacher, Pauline McCann, a black concert pianist and singer.

Of course, there was the inevitable role, Which I used to listen to all the time, and I was amazed because I didn't…

378.t: Quitting lessons after a rap on the knuckles
378.s: A teacher hit his hands with a ruler for playing by ear, so he never went back; his mother let him decide, and the Hammond organ came later.

89.t: Piano lessons at ten for fifty cents
89.s: He began piano around age ten, taking weekly home lessons from a teacher who proudly drove a new Ford.
89.q: Well, I began piano when I was about ten years old and I studied piano for four years. One of my teachers was a descendent of the great Rafer Johnson, the decathlon winner from some years ago at Antioch Collech in Yellow Springs, Ohio. I remember he used to come up to the house -- come all the way…

758.s: Roy quit piano after a teacher who slapped his hands frightened him.

384.s: He studied piano with Sister Gabriel, won the school band drum chair from Susanne Lenz, and says his father, a pianist, gave him no lessons.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: Specht, Weems and learning to play

148.t: Mother's brutal teaching and his resentment of teachers
148.s: His mother taught him miserably until he kicked a hole in the piano; he quit music for years and came to resent every teacher, learning instead from other musicians.
148.q: My mother started to train me and she was an impossible teacher, she made it pure hell for me. I kicked a hole in the piano one day, ran out and that was the end of my musical training--at least by my mother. There was a real upheaval in the house at the time, my father and mother got into a big…

95.t: Learning organ and piano at home
95.s: She learned on the organ her mother had at home, later got a piano, and taught herself with her brother George helping.
95.ch: Second day: early memories, London 1966 and other singers
95.q: My aunt or somebody, I don't remember. But I know Mama had an organ. I don't know (unintelligible). See, my cousin was always (unintelligible). Then my cousin gave my Mama a piano.

75.t: First piano lessons and imitation by ear
75.s: A house-call teacher with no ear gave him 50-cent lessons; he imitated tunes on his grandmother's piano and had no formal training until Miss Stiller at the Henrietta School.
75.q: No, I started with a teacher, you know, who came to the house -- who later I found out didn't have an ear at all! He used to teach the kids. He used to come to their houses and give a 50-cent lesson.

76.t: Marge's piano lessons, ragtime and East St. Louis
76.s: Marge studied piano for three years by the Czerny method and learned ragtime from Frank Eubanks, who learned it from Jelly Roll Morton. They clarify that East St. Louis is across the bridge in Illinois.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band

125.ch: Early listening, piano and adolescent conflict
125.q: Well, I didn't consider the Mills Brothers to be exactly jazz, although -- yes, I would have to consider in the field of jazz, yes. But now --

239.t: Piano teachers: Josephus Robinson and the lady who caught him playing by ear
239.s: Piano as a bigger challenge, his first piano teachers, church recitals, and playing lessons by ear.
